lessonTitle: Peripheral Nerve Injuries of the Upper Limb

blocks.text: A woman in her fifties wakes at night with burning, tingling fingers that ease when she shakes her hand. Over months the base of her thumb becomes flat and she drops cups. A single nerve, compressed in a narrow tunnel at the wrist, produces this whole story, and knowing the nerve's territory lets you work out the lesion from the signs.

blocks.markdown: Each peripheral nerve has a **motor distribution** (the muscles it supplies) and a **sensory distribution** (the skin it supplies). If you know these, you can predict what is lost when a nerve is cut, stretched or compressed at a known site, and you can work backwards from a patient's weakness and numbness to the nerve and the level of injury. Clinical examination of the upper limb is therefore a systematic motor and sensory screen of four nerves: median, ulnar, radial and axillary.

rows: Most forearm flexors and pronators (not flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus); thenar muscles; lateral two lumbricals
Palmar skin of the thumb, index, middle and lateral half of the ring finger, and the lateral palm; dorsal skin over the distal parts of those fingers
Flexor carpi ulnaris; ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus; hypothenar muscles; all interossei; adductor pollicis; medial two lumbricals
Medial one and a half fingers (palmar and dorsal) and the medial palm
Triceps; brachioradialis; all forearm extensors; supinator
Posterior arm and forearm; dorsum of the lateral hand, especially the first web space
Skin over the lower part of deltoid (regimental badge area)
blocks.caption: Motor and sensory territories of the four main upper-limb nerves.

blocks.title: Peripheral nerve injury
blocks.text: Damage to a peripheral nerve by compression, stretch, laceration or ischaemia. A complete lesion causes flaccid paralysis of the muscles supplied, loss of sensation in the skin supplied, and later muscle wasting. Because sensory territories overlap, the loss may be smaller than the nominal distribution (autonomous zones are the small areas supplied by one nerve only).

blocks.markdown: **Median nerve at the carpal tunnel.** The median nerve passes under the flexor retinaculum with the nine flexor tendons (four flexor digitorum superficialis, four flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus). Swelling or thickening in the tunnel compresses the nerve: this is **carpal tunnel syndrome**. The recurrent (thenar) branch is affected, so the thenar muscles waste and thumb abduction and opposition are weak (LOAF muscles: lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis; in carpal tunnel the lumbricals and thenar muscles are affected). Sensation is lost over the lateral three and a half digits, but the skin of the **thenar eminence is spared**, because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to it, so it escapes compression.

blocks.title: Locating a median nerve lesion
blocks.prompt: Patient A cannot flex the distal phalanx of the thumb or index finger and has weak pronation; patient B has only thenar wasting and numb finger pulps, with normal pronation. Where is each lesion?

steps.text: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (arising in the forearm) supplies flexor pollicis longus, lateral flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus; pronator teres is supplied higher up.
Patient A: weak pronation and weak flexion of the thumb and index finger imply a lesion proximal to the origin of these branches, in the forearm or at the elbow.
Patient B: pronation normal means branches to forearm muscles are intact; only the distal median nerve is affected, i.e. at the wrist (carpal tunnel).

blocks.answer: Patient A has a proximal median nerve lesion (forearm or elbow); patient B has a distal lesion at the carpal tunnel.

blocks.markdown: **Ulnar nerve at the elbow.** The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle (the 'funny bone') where it is superficial and exposed to fractures and direct blows. A lesion there paralyses the interossei, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis and the medial two lumbricals, with loss of sensation over the medial one and a half fingers. Weakness of the lumbricals (which flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints) leaves the long extensors and flexors unopposed, producing a **claw hand** of the ring and little fingers. With adductor pollicis paralysed, a patient gripping a piece of paper between thumb and index finger compensates by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint with flexor pollicis longus (median nerve): this is **Froment sign**.

**Radial nerve at the humeral shaft.** The radial nerve runs in the radial (spiral) groove on the posterior humerus, where it is vulnerable to a midshaft fracture. The branches to triceps leave proximal to the groove, so **triceps is spared**, but the forearm extensors are paralysed, producing **wrist drop**; sensory loss is usually limited to a small area over the dorsum of the first web space, because of overlap from neighbouring nerves. **Axillary nerve:** winding around the surgical neck of the humerus, it is injured in fractures of the neck or anterior shoulder dislocation, causing weak abduction (after the first 15 degrees) and numbness over the lower deltoid.

rows: Thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction and opposition, numbness of lateral three and a half digits with sparing of the thenar eminence skin
Fracture of the medial epicondyle, repeated pressure
Claw hand, weak finger abduction and adduction, Froment sign, numbness of medial one and a half fingers
Wrist drop, triceps spared, loss of sensation over dorsum of first web space
Weak abduction, flat shoulder contour, numb lower deltoid skin
blocks.caption: Common sites and signs of upper-limb nerve injury.

blocks.title: Systematic screen of the upper limb nerves
blocks.text: Test each nerve for both motor and sensory function. Motor: radial, extend the wrist and fingers against resistance; median, abduct the thumb at right angles to the palm (abductor pollicis brevis), or make an OK sign (anterior interosseous); ulnar, spread the fingers against resistance (dorsal interossei) or grip a card between the fingers; axillary, palpate deltoid while the patient abducts the arm. Sensory: radial, first dorsal web space; median, pulp of the index finger; ulnar, pulp of the little finger; axillary, regimental badge area.

blocks.title: From signs to nerve
blocks.prompt: After a fracture of the medial epicondyle, a man cannot spread his fingers and has numbness of the little finger. Which nerve is injured, and how would you test it?

steps.text: Finger abduction is by the dorsal interossei, which are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
The little finger is in the ulnar sensory territory, and the medial epicondyle is a known site where the ulnar nerve is exposed.
Test by asking the patient to spread the fingers against resistance, and test pinprick sensation on the pulp of the little finger.

blocks.answer: Ulnar nerve; test finger abduction and sensation of the little finger.

items: Median nerve lesion at the wrist: thenar wasting, loss of thumb opposition, numb lateral three and a half digits.
Ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow: claw hand, Froment sign, numb medial one and a half fingers.
Radial nerve lesion at the humeral shaft: wrist drop, triceps spared.
Axillary nerve lesion: weak abduction, numb lower deltoid.

blocks.title: Level matters
blocks.text: A claw hand is more obvious with a distal ulnar lesion than with a high one, because a high lesion also paralyses the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, which weakens the flexion that produces the claw. Always consider the level of injury and which muscles are included.

points: Learn each nerve's motor and sensory territory, then predict deficits from the site of injury.

Median nerve at the carpal tunnel: thenar weakness and loss of sensation in the lateral three and a half digits with thenar skin sparing; ulnar nerve at the elbow: claw hand and Froment sign; radial nerve at the humeral shaft: wrist drop with triceps spared; axillary nerve: weak abduction and numb lower deltoid.
A systematic screen tests one muscle action and one skin area for each nerve.

questions.stem: In carpal tunnel syndrome, why is the skin over the thenar eminence usually spared?

options.text: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to it
The thenar eminence is supplied by the ulnar nerve
The radial nerve supplies the thenar eminence
The median nerve does not carry sensory fibres to the palm

questions.correctOptionText: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to it

distractorRationale.b: The ulnar nerve supplies the medial palm, not the thenar skin.
distractorRationale.c: The radial nerve supplies skin on the dorsum of the hand.
distractorRationale.d: The median nerve does carry sensation from the palm and lateral digits.

questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve in the distal forearm, before the nerve enters the carpal tunnel, and passes over the retinaculum. Compression within the tunnel therefore spares the thenar skin while affecting the digital branches.

questions.stem: A man has wrist drop after a fracture of the midshaft of the humerus. Which nerve has been injured?

distractorRationale.b: Median nerve injury causes thumb and finger flexor weakness.
distractorRationale.c: Ulnar nerve injury causes claw hand.
distractorRationale.d: The axillary nerve is at the surgical neck, not the midshaft.

questions.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the posterior humerus and supplies the wrist and finger extensors, so injury produces wrist drop. Triceps is usually spared because its branches leave proximal to the groove.

questions.stem: Which muscle is usually spared in a radial nerve injury at the humeral shaft?

distractorRationale.b: Extensor carpi radialis longus is paralysed by a lesion distal to the groove.
distractorRationale.c: Brachioradialis is supplied by a branch distal to the groove.
distractorRationale.d: Supinator is supplied by the deep branch distal to the groove.

questions.explanation: The branches to triceps leave the radial nerve in the axilla and upper arm, before the nerve enters the spiral groove. A lesion in the groove therefore spares triceps but paralyses the forearm extensors.

questions.stem: After a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, a patient cannot abduct or adduct the fingers and has numbness of the little finger. Which test best confirms motor loss from this nerve?

distractorRationale.b: Wrist extension tests the radial nerve.
distractorRationale.c: Arm abduction tests the axillary nerve (and supraspinatus).
distractorRationale.d: Elbow flexion tests the musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.explanation: Finger abduction is by the dorsal interossei, which are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, where it is exposed to injury.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old has a deep wrist laceration. He cannot oppose his thumb and has numbness of the palmar surface of the thumb, index and middle fingers. Which nerve is injured?

distractorRationale.b: Ulnar nerve loss would affect the medial one and a half digits.
distractorRationale.c: Radial nerve loss would affect the dorsum of the hand and wrist extension.
distractorRationale.d: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and does not reach the hand.

questions.explanation: Thumb opposition is by opponens pollicis, a thenar muscle supplied by the median nerve, and the palmar skin of the lateral three and a half digits is median territory. A laceration at the wrist injures this nerve distally.

questions.stem: True or false: adductor pollicis is supplied by the median nerve.

distractorRationale.a: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

questions.explanation: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, which is why Froment sign appears in ulnar nerve lesions. The thenar muscles, not adductor pollicis, are supplied by the median nerve.

questions.stem: Numbness over the skin of the lower deltoid (regimental badge area) suggests injury to which nerve?

distractorRationale.b: The suprascapular nerve is motor to two rotator cuff muscles and carries no skin from this area.
distractorRationale.c: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the lateral forearm skin.
distractorRationale.d: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior and is purely motor.

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve gives the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm to the skin over the lower deltoid. It also supplies deltoid and teres minor, so injury also causes weak abduction.

questions.stem: Why is the claw hand often less obvious in a high ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow than in a distal lesion at the wrist?

options.text: A high lesion also paralyses the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, which weakens the flexion of the fingers that produces the claw
A high lesion spares the interossei
A high lesion affects the radial nerve as well
A high lesion paralyses the extensors of the fingers

questions.correctOptionText: A high lesion also paralyses the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, which weakens the flexion of the fingers that produces the claw

distractorRationale.b: The interossei are paralysed in both high and low lesions.
distractorRationale.c: The radial nerve is not involved in the elbow ulnar lesion.
distractorRationale.d: The extensors are supplied by the radial nerve and are not paralysed.

questions.explanation: Claw hand results from unopposed long extensors and flexors after loss of the lumbricals. In a high lesion, the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is also lost, so the flexion of the ring and little fingers at the distal joints is weak and the claw looks less marked.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has night-time tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, followed by wasting at the base of the thumb. Identify the nerve and lesion site, state the muscles and skin affected, and explain why the thenar eminence skin is spared.
markingGuide: Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum.
Thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis) and the lateral two lumbricals weakened.
Sensory loss over the palmar lateral three and a half digits.
Thenar eminence skin spared because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the retinaculum and passes superficially.
Late features: thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction and opposition.
questions.explanation: Compression within the tunnel affects the recurrent motor branch and the digital sensory branches but not the palmar cutaneous branch. The distribution of signs therefore points precisely to the carpal tunnel rather than to a higher lesion.

questions.stem: Describe a systematic motor and sensory screen of the median, ulnar, radial and axillary nerves in the upper limb, giving one motor test and one sensory area for each nerve.
markingGuide: Radial: wrist extension against resistance; sensory test at the dorsum of the first web space.
Median: thumb abduction at right angles to the palm (or OK sign for the anterior interosseous branch); sensory test at the pulp of the index finger.
Ulnar: spreading the fingers against resistance (or Froment test); sensory test at the pulp of the little finger.
Axillary: contraction of deltoid during abduction; sensory test over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area).
questions.explanation: A systematic screen uses one reliable muscle action and one autonomous skin area for each nerve, which makes comparison with the other side easy. It also allows you to localise a lesion by which branches are involved.
